title: Forgot your Google password? Now you can log in with a selfie.
gist: Google added selfie-video-based account recovery/sign-in, letting users regain access with facial verification instead of only recovery contacts or backup codes; the feature is opt-in, excluded from Workspace/child/Advanced Protection accounts, and Google claims layered deepfake-detection despite acknowledging real-time deepfake video is now feasible.

insights.claim: Google now lets users set up account recovery and sign-in via a recorded selfie video, stored encrypted on Google's servers, as an alternative to recovery contacts or backup codes.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Marks a mainstream consumer platform normalizing biometric video as an account-security factor, a trend other identity/authentication vendors will likely be pressured to match.
insights.quote: You can now give Google a video record of your face and sign into your account with a selfie

insights.claim: Selfie sign-in is unavailable for Google Workspace accounts, child accounts, and any account enrolled in Google's Advanced Protection Program, which instead requires a physical security key.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Google itself is signaling the feature is not considered secure enough for its highest-risk account tier, an implicit admission the method trades security for convenience.
insights.quote: You won't be able to configure selfie sign-ins for Workspace accounts, child accounts, or any account enrolled in Google's Advanced Protection Program.

insights.claim: Beyond login recovery, Google can use the same selfie video for age verification on certain account features and to generate an AI avatar, with a separate opt-in toggle allowing Google to use the video to improve its facial-recognition models.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Reveals Google is building a multi-purpose biometric data asset (recovery, age-gating, AI avatar generation, model training) from a single consumer capture flow — relevant to privacy-regulation and data-monetization watchers.
insights.quote: Selfie videos can be used for login purposes, to verify your age for accessing certain account features, and to create an AI avatar.

insights.claim: Google verifies liveness during selfie sign-in by having the user move their head and matching that motion against the stored video, but the author notes deepfake video generation, including near-real-time deepfakes, is now technically feasible and could threaten this liveness check.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Highlights a live security gap in consumer biometric authentication as generative AI video tools improve — an emerging attack surface for account-takeover fraud that security vendors and platforms will need to address.
insights.quote: in the age of AI, it's not very hard to make deepfake videos of someone. It's even possible to do that in near real-time, as would be required for Google account recovery.

insights.claim: Google claims to employ multiple layers of security measures to detect deepfakes attempting to spoof selfie sign-in, but the author frames this defense as less secure than other recovery options, evidenced by Google excluding Advanced Protection users from the feature.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Signals that even Google's own risk model treats selfie-based recovery as a lower-assurance tier, useful context when assessing security posture of platforms adopting similar biometric-recovery features.
insights.quote: Google claims it has multiple layers of security measures to detect deepfakes, but this method may not be as secure as other options.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Google claims it has multiple layers'
